gt.en: Students had parties and bought small gifts for themselves.
gt.zh: 學生們開派對，還買小禮物送給自己。

gt.en: In 2009, a big online shopping company started selling things at low prices on that day.
gt.zh: 2009 年，一家大型網路購物公司開始在那天低價賣東西。

gt.en: Soon, millions of people were shopping online on November 11.
gt.zh: 很快地，數百萬人在十一月十一日上網購物。

gt.en: In Taiwan, many online shops also have 11/11 sales.
gt.zh: 在台灣，許多網路商店也有雙十一特價。

b.title: How a Student Joke Became a Shopping Giant
text: Singles' Day began in the 1990s as a joke among university students in Nanjing, China. Because the date 11/11 is made up of four ones, they adopted it as a day to celebrate being single.
In 2009 the e-commerce company Alibaba saw a business opportunity and held a one-day online sale. Only a few dozen brands took part, but the idea caught on fast.

Within a decade, Singles' Day had grown into the world's largest shopping event, far bigger than America's Black Friday. Sales were counted live on giant screens, and in 2021 Alibaba reported orders worth over 80 billion US dollars during the festival period.
The event spread across Asia, including Taiwan, where online platforms now offer 11/11 discounts.
Its critics point to the costs. Mountains of packaging create waste, delivery vehicles add pollution, and clever marketing encourages impulse buying — purchases people later regret.
In recent years the festival has become quieter, as companies stopped announcing record totals and shoppers became more careful with money.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Singles' Day began as a student joke and grew into a giant shopping event, with both benefits and costs.
In 2021, Alibaba reported orders worth over 80 billion US dollars.
Singles' Day is now bigger than Black Friday in America.
Students in Nanjing chose 11/11 because it has four ones.
q.why: 只有第二項涵蓋起源、成長與代價。

q.q: How many brands took part in the first sale in 2009?
opts: A few hundred
Several thousand
Every brand in China
Only a few dozen
q.why: 第二段：Only a few dozen brands took part。

q.q: Which is NOT mentioned as a cost of the festival?
opts: Packaging waste
Shops closing because of low prices
Pollution from delivery vehicles
Impulse buying
q.why: 第五段列出包裝、汙染、衝動購物；沒有提到商店倒閉。

q.q: In paragraph 5, “impulse buying” means buying things ___.
opts: only after comparing many prices
in large amounts to save money
suddenly, without careful thought
for other people as gifts
q.why: impulse buying = 衝動購物。

q.q: What does the last paragraph suggest about the festival today?
opts: It is growing faster than ever
It has been replaced by Black Friday
It is now only for single people
It has become less showy as companies and shoppers changed
q.why: 最後一段：the festival has become quieter。

q.q: An online shop shows a countdown: “Only 5 minutes left! Buy now!” Based on the text, why might this be a problem?
opts: It creates pressure that can lead to impulse buying
It means the products are low quality
It makes delivery slower
It is against the law in Taiwan
q.why: 倒數製造急迫感，促成文章提到的衝動購物。

tr.en: Because the date 11/11 is made up of four ones, they adopted it as a day to celebrate being single.
tr.zh: 因為 11/11 這個日期是由四個一組成的，他們就把它當作慶祝單身的日子。

tr.en: In 2009 the e-commerce company Alibaba saw a business opportunity and held a one-day online sale.
tr.zh: 2009 年，電子商務公司阿里巴巴看到了商機，舉辦了一場為期一天的網路特賣。

tr.en: Mountains of packaging create waste, delivery vehicles add pollution, and clever marketing encourages impulse buying — purchases people later regret.
tr.zh: 堆積如山的包裝製造了垃圾，送貨車輛增加了汙染，而聰明的行銷手法則鼓勵衝動購物——也就是人們事後會後悔的購買。

c.title: The Business of Being Alone
text: Few commercial phenomena illustrate the inventiveness of modern marketing as neatly as Singles' Day. What began in the 1990s as a self-mocking ritual among Nanjing university students, who chose 11/11 for its four solitary ones, has been transformed into the largest retail event on the planet.

The pivotal moment came in 2009, when Alibaba repackaged the date as an online sale. The company understood that a festival without traditions could be filled with whatever meaning sold best, and it supplied gala shows, countdowns and real-time sales tallies that turned shopping into a spectator sport.
By 2021 the reported value of orders exceeded 80 billion US dollars, dwarfing America's Black Friday.

Success, however, attracted scrutiny. Environmental groups highlighted the packaging generated by billions of parcels, economists noted how artificial urgency fuels impulsive spending, and regulators grew wary of the platforms' power.

Since then the event has grown more subdued; companies stopped trumpeting record totals and consumers have become more frugal. Singles' Day thus offers a compact lesson in how a date can be manufactured into a festival — and how the meaning a market creates can also, gradually, be questioned.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Singles' Day is an ancient Chinese tradition that Alibaba revived.
Singles' Day shows how marketing can turn a date into a huge festival, and how that meaning can later be questioned.
Online shopping festivals are harmful and should be banned.
Singles' Day became popular because single people are lonely.
q.why: 主旨：行銷能把日期打造成節慶，這種意義也可能被質疑。

q.q: In paragraph 5, “frugal” means ___.
opts: careful not to spend much money
eager to buy new things
suspicious of companies
loyal to one brand
q.why: frugal = 節儉的。

q.q: Why does the writer say a festival “without traditions could be filled with whatever meaning sold best”?
opts: Because traditional festivals are not allowed to have sales
Because students had already planned the meaning
Because the government chose the meaning
Because a new festival had no fixed meaning, so a company could shape it to encourage buying
q.why: 第二段：沒有傳統包袱的節日，可以被填入最好賣的意義。

q.q: How does the writer view Singles' Day?
opts: Enthusiastic — it is a model for every country
Hostile — it is purely harmful
Analytical — impressed by its inventiveness but aware of its costs
Neutral — the writer gives no opinion
q.why: 既讚嘆行銷創意，也指出環境與消費問題。

q.q: How is the essay organised?
opts: Problem → solution → result
A comparison of Singles' Day and Black Friday throughout
Origin → commercial transformation → scale → criticism → recent change and lesson
Criticism first, then the history
q.why: 結構：起源 → 商業化 → 規模 → 批評 → 近年變化與啟示。

q.q: Which modern example is MOST similar to how Singles' Day was created?
opts: A traditional festival that families have celebrated for centuries
A company inventing “Pet Love Day” with discounts on pet products
A national holiday chosen to remember a war
A school sports day planned by students
q.why: 雙十一是企業把一個日期包裝成購物節；公司自創節日促銷最相似。

discuss: Have you or your family ever bought something on 11/11? Was it something you really needed?
How can shoppers avoid impulse buying when there are big sales?
Do you think online shopping festivals are good or bad for the environment? What could companies do better?

zh: 佩特拉：玫瑰色的古城
src: UNESCO · National Geographic · The New York Times

a.title: A City Cut into the Rocks
text: Petra is an old city in the desert of Jordan. Its buildings are not built with bricks. They are cut into the pink and red rocks!
People called the Nabataeans made the city more than 2,000 years ago.
To enter Petra, you walk through a long, narrow path between high rocks. It is called the Siq.
At the end of the path, you see a beautiful building called the Treasury. It is very tall.
The Nabataeans were clever with water. They made channels to catch rain in the dry desert.
Today, many tourists visit Petra. Some ride camels or donkeys to see more of the old city.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: The narrow path called the Siq
An ancient city carved into rocks in Jordan
How the Nabataeans collected rain
Tourists riding camels in the desert
q.why: 全文介紹佩特拉古城；其他都是細節。

q.q: What is the Siq?
opts: A tall building at the end of the path
A channel that carries rainwater
The name of the people who built Petra
A long, narrow path between high rocks
q.why: 第三段：a long, narrow path between high rocks. It is called the Siq。

q.q: How did the Nabataeans get water in the dry desert?
opts: They carried it from the sea on camels
They dug deep wells under the Treasury
They made channels to catch rain
They bought water from other cities
q.why: 第五段：They made channels to catch rain。

q.q: In the text, “narrow” means ___.
opts: not wide
very long
very high
dark and cold
q.why: narrow = 狹窄的。

q.q: Why is Petra different from most cities?
opts: It was built only for tourists
It has no water at all
Its buildings are cut into the rock instead of built with bricks
It was built by people from Europe
q.why: 第一段：cut into the pink and red rocks!

q.q: You are making a travel plan for Petra. Based on the text, what should you plan to do FIRST when you arrive?
opts: Walk through the Siq to reach the Treasury
Visit the water channels on the top of the Treasury
Ride a camel into the Treasury
Take a boat along the river
q.why: 第三、四段：要進入佩特拉先走過蛇道，盡頭才看到寶庫。

gt.en: Petra is an old city in the desert of Jordan.
gt.zh: 佩特拉是約旦沙漠裡的一座古城。

gt.en: To enter Petra, you walk through a long, narrow path between high rocks.
gt.zh: 要進入佩特拉，你得走過一條夾在高聳岩石之間、又長又窄的小路。

gt.en: The Nabataeans were clever with water.
gt.zh: 納巴泰人很懂得運用水。

gt.en: Today, many tourists visit Petra.
gt.zh: 今天，許多觀光客來參觀佩特拉。

b.title: Hidden City of the Desert
text: Hidden among the mountains of southern Jordan, Petra is one of the most astonishing archaeological sites on Earth. Its temples and tombs were carved directly into rose-coloured sandstone cliffs.
The city was the capital of the Nabataeans, Arab traders who grew wealthy by controlling caravan routes that carried incense and spices across the desert more than two thousand years ago.

Visitors enter through the Siq, a winding canyon about a kilometre long whose walls rise as high as 80 metres. At its end, the facade of Al-Khazneh, known as the Treasury, suddenly appears in the sunlight.
Despite the dry climate, the Nabataeans supported a large population by building dams, cisterns and channels to collect and store rainwater.

After trade routes shifted and earthquakes struck, Petra slowly declined. For centuries it was known mainly to local Bedouin, until a Swiss traveller, Johann Ludwig Burckhardt, described it to Europeans in 1812.
Today Petra is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and Jordan works to balance tourism with the need to protect the fragile stone.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: The Treasury is a famous building carved into the cliffs of Petra.
Burckhardt was the first person ever to find Petra.
The Nabataeans grew rich by trading incense and spices.
Petra, an ancient trading capital carved into stone, is now a protected world treasure.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文；其他是部分細節或錯誤說法。

q.q: How did the Nabataeans become wealthy?
opts: By controlling caravan routes for incense and spices
By selling the rose-coloured stone
By charging tourists to enter the Siq
By farming the desert with rainwater
q.why: 第二段：controlling caravan routes that carried incense and spices。

q.q: Why did Petra decline?
opts: The water channels dried up suddenly
Burckhardt took its treasures to Europe
Trade routes shifted and earthquakes struck
Too many tourists damaged it
q.why: 第五段：After trade routes shifted and earthquakes struck。

q.q: In paragraph 3, a “canyon” is ___.
opts: a wide, flat desert
a deep, narrow valley with steep sides
a carved stone building
a road built by traders
q.why: canyon = 峽谷。

q.q: What does the writer suggest by saying Petra was known mainly to local Bedouin?
opts: The Bedouin built Petra
It was not truly lost; Burckhardt made it known to Europeans
No one lived near Petra for centuries
The Bedouin kept it secret from Burckhardt
q.why: 當地人一直知道它，布克哈特是讓歐洲人知道。

q.q: Which plan best matches the text's idea of balancing tourism and protection at Petra?
opts: Limit visitor numbers and keep people on set paths
Allow unlimited visitors because tourism brings money
Close Petra to everyone forever
Rebuild the old buildings with new stone
q.why: 最後一段：balance tourism with the need to protect the fragile stone——限制人數、固定路線最平衡。

tr.en: Hidden among the mountains of southern Jordan, Petra is one of the most astonishing archaeological sites on Earth.
tr.zh: 隱藏在約旦南部群山之間的佩特拉，是地球上最令人驚嘆的考古遺址之一。

tr.en: Visitors enter through the Siq, a winding canyon about a kilometre long whose walls rise as high as 80 metres.
tr.zh: 遊客從「蛇道」進入，這是一條大約一公里長的蜿蜒峽谷，兩側的岩壁高達八十公尺。

tr.en: After trade routes shifted and earthquakes struck, Petra slowly declined.
tr.zh: 在貿易路線改變、又遭遇地震之後，佩特拉慢慢地衰落了。

c.title: Wealth Carved in Stone
text: Petra is often described as a lost city, but its real story is one of calculated prosperity. Carved into the rose-red sandstone of southern Jordan, it served as the capital of the Nabataeans, who grew rich by taxing and protecting the caravans that carried incense, myrrh and spices between Arabia and the Mediterranean.

The approach is pure theatre. Visitors thread their way through the Siq, a narrow gorge whose walls tower above them, until the facade of Al-Khazneh, the so-called Treasury, bursts into view, its columns cut, not built, from the living rock.

Less photogenic but more remarkable was the city's hydraulic engineering. In an arid landscape, the Nabataeans built dams, terracotta pipes and cisterns that captured flash floods and sustained a population of perhaps tens of thousands.

Petra's decline was gradual rather than sudden: Roman annexation, shifting trade routes toward the sea and devastating earthquakes eroded its importance until only Bedouin herders remained to know it.

Today, its popularity poses a quieter threat. Salt, wind and millions of footsteps wear at the soft stone, and conservationists argue that preserving Petra requires limiting the very admiration that keeps it famous.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: Petra was suddenly destroyed by one great earthquake.
Petra's most important feature is the Treasury's facade.
Petra's story is one of clever prosperity and slow decline, and today its fame itself threatens it.
Petra survived because no one ever visited it.
q.why: 主旨：精明的繁榮與緩慢衰落，如今名氣本身成為威脅。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “arid” means ___.
opts: very dry
very rocky
very hot
very empty
q.why: arid = 乾旱的。

q.q: Why does the writer call Petra's water system “more remarkable” than the Treasury?
opts: The water system is older than the Treasury
Tourists prefer to visit the water system
The Treasury was built by the Romans
Supporting a large population in a dry landscape was a greater achievement than a beautiful facade
q.why: 第三段：在乾旱地區養活大量人口，比華麗外觀更了不起。

q.q: How does the writer describe the entrance through the Siq?
opts: As tiring and dangerous
As dramatic, like theatre
As disappointing compared with photos
As purely practical
q.why: 第二段：The approach is pure theatre。

q.q: What irony does the final paragraph point out?
opts: Petra became famous only after it declined
Protecting Petra may require limiting the admiration that keeps it famous
The Nabataeans' water system now damages the stone
Tourists prefer modern buildings to ancient ones
q.why: 結尾：preserving Petra requires limiting the very admiration that keeps it famous。

q.q: Which piece of evidence would BEST support the writer's claim that popularity threatens Petra?
opts: A record of how many camels live near Petra
A photo of the Treasury at sunset
A study showing the soft stone wears faster on the most-visited paths
A list of films made at Petra
q.why: 作者說人潮的腳步磨損軟石；顯示熱門路段磨損較快的研究最能支持。

discuss: Why do you think the Nabataeans carved their buildings into rock instead of building with bricks?
Should famous places like Petra limit the number of visitors? What are the good and bad sides?
If you could visit one ancient city in the world, which would you choose and why?

zh: 世界善意日：小小善意的大力量

a.title: Small Acts, Big Smiles
text: November 13 is World Kindness Day. It is a day to be kind to others.
Kindness can be very simple. You can smile at someone, help a classmate, or say thank you.
You can hold the door for someone, or share your snack with a friend.
When you are kind, other people feel happy. Scientists say it can make you feel happy too!
Kindness can also spread. When one person is kind, others often want to be kind too.
What kind thing can you do today?

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How scientists study happiness
World Kindness Day and simple ways to be kind
How to share snacks with friends
Why people should always hold the door
q.why: 全文介紹世界善意日與簡單的善行；其他是例子。

q.q: Which is given as an example of kindness?
opts: Giving someone money
Doing a classmate's homework
Buying expensive gifts
Saying thank you
q.why: 第二段：say thank you。

q.q: What do scientists say about being kind?
opts: It can make you feel happy too
It only helps the other person
It is good only for children
It makes people tired
q.why: 第四段：it can make you feel happy too!

q.q: In the text, “spread” means ___.
opts: to stay with one person
to stop after a short time
to move from one person to others
to become smaller
q.why: spread = 傳播、擴散。

q.q: Why does the text end with a question?
opts: To test whether readers remember the date
To show the writer is not sure what kindness is
To make readers think about doing something kind
To start a quiz
q.why: 結尾問題邀請讀者行動。

q.q: Which situation best shows kindness “spreading” as the text describes?
opts: Amy helps Ben, and later Ben helps a new student
Amy helps Ben, and Ben says thank you
Amy shares her snack because she is full
Amy holds the door because her teacher asked her to
q.why: 文章說善意會傳開：一人善待後，別人也想善待他人——A 幫 B、B 再幫別人。

gt.en: It is a day to be kind to others.
gt.zh: 這是一個善待別人的日子。

gt.en: Kindness can be very simple.
gt.zh: 善意可以非常簡單。

gt.en: You can hold the door for someone, or share your snack with a friend.
gt.zh: 你可以幫別人扶著門，或是和朋友分享你的點心。

gt.en: When you are kind, other people feel happy.
gt.zh: 當你待人友善，別人就會覺得開心。

b.title: Why Kindness Is Contagious
text: World Kindness Day, held every November 13, was introduced in 1998 by the World Kindness Movement, a group that grew out of a conference in Tokyo the year before.
The idea is simple: to encourage people everywhere to notice others and do something good for them, without expecting anything back.

Research suggests that kindness benefits the giver as well as the receiver. Studies have found that people who spend money or time on others often report feeling happier than those who spend it only on themselves.
Kindness also appears to be contagious. In experiments, people who received help were more likely to help someone else later, creating a chain of generosity.
Small acts count. Including a lonely classmate, writing a thank-you note or simply listening carefully can change someone's day.
Of course, kindness is not the same as always saying yes. Being kind sometimes means being honest or standing up for someone who is being treated unfairly.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: World Kindness Day started at a conference in Tokyo.
Kind people should always say yes to others.
Spending money on others is the best way to be happy.
Kindness helps both the giver and the receiver and can spread from person to person.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文；第二項是細節；第三、四項與文意不符或太絕對。

q.q: Where did the World Kindness Movement grow out of?
opts: A school project in Taiwan
A science study in America
A conference in Tokyo
A UN meeting in 1998
q.why: 第一段：grew out of a conference in Tokyo。

q.q: What did experiments show about people who received help?
opts: They felt they had to pay the helper back
They were more likely to help someone else later
They became less independent
They forgot the help quickly
q.why: 第四段：more likely to help someone else later。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “contagious” means ___.
opts: able to spread from one person to another
harmful to your health
easy to forget
only shared with friends
q.why: contagious = 會傳染的。

q.q: What does the last paragraph suggest?
opts: Kind people should avoid disagreeing
Real kindness can include honesty and standing up for others
Kindness means doing whatever others ask
Being honest is less important than being nice
q.why: 最後一段：Being kind sometimes means being honest or standing up for someone。

q.q: A classmate is being laughed at by a group. According to the text, which action is the kindest?
opts: Laugh a little so the group doesn't target you
Ignore it because it is not your problem
Tell the classmate later that you felt sorry
Calmly tell the group to stop and stand with the classmate
q.why: 最後一段：仁慈有時是挺身為受到不公平對待的人說話。

tr.en: The idea is simple: to encourage people everywhere to notice others and do something good for them, without expecting anything back.
tr.zh: 這個想法很簡單：鼓勵各地的人留意身邊的人，為他們做點好事，而且不求回報。

tr.en: Research suggests that kindness benefits the giver as well as the receiver.
tr.zh: 研究顯示，善意不只對接受的人有好處，對付出的人也有好處。

tr.en: In experiments, people who received help were more likely to help someone else later, creating a chain of generosity.
tr.zh: 在實驗中，得到幫助的人後來比較可能去幫助別人，形成一條慷慨的連鎖。

c.title: The Quiet Economics of Kindness
text: Kindness is easy to dismiss as sentimental, a soft virtue for greeting cards. World Kindness Day, observed every November 13 since the World Kindness Movement proposed it in 1998, invites a more serious look.

Behavioural research has repeatedly found that prosocial spending — devoting money or time to others — is associated with greater wellbeing than equivalent spending on oneself. The effect appears across very different cultures, which suggests it is not merely a local custom.

Kindness also seems to propagate. Experiments on 'paying it forward' show that recipients of generosity are more inclined to extend it to strangers, so that a single act can ripple outward through a network of people who never meet.
None of this makes kindness simple. Genuine kindness can demand courage: telling an uncomfortable truth, refusing to join in mockery, or defending someone whom the group has decided to exclude.
Seen this way, kindness is less a mood than a practice — an everyday choice that, multiplied across a community, quietly shapes whether people feel safe enough to trust one another.
gloss: 多愁善感的；感情用事的

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Kindness is mainly about spending money on others.
Research shows kindness works only in some cultures.
Kindness is a pleasant feeling rather than an action.
Kindness is a serious everyday practice that benefits individuals and builds trust in communities.
q.why: 主旨：善意是值得認真看待的日常實踐。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “propagate” means ___.
opts: to measure
to spread
to reward
to decrease
q.why: propagate = 傳播。

q.q: Why does the writer mention that the effect appears across different cultures?
opts: To suggest the link between kindness and happiness is not just a local custom
To show that every culture practises kindness in the same way
To argue that some cultures are kinder than others
To explain where the World Kindness Movement began
q.why: 第二段：not merely a local custom。

q.q: How does the writer treat the view that kindness is “sentimental”?
opts: As fully accurate
As a scientific finding
As a view worth challenging
As the writer's own belief
q.why: 作者先提出這種看法，再要求 a more serious look。

q.q: How does the final paragraph redefine kindness?
opts: As a type of spending
As a reaction to others' kindness
As a personality trait you are born with
As a practice and choice rather than just a mood
q.why: 結尾：kindness is less a mood than a practice。

q.q: A school wants to measure whether a “Kindness Week” worked. Which measure fits the writer's view best?
opts: Surveying whether students feel safer and more able to trust each other
Counting how many kindness posters were made
Checking how much money students donated
Asking teachers which students are the nicest
q.why: 結尾：善意累積起來會影響人們是否覺得安全、能互相信任。

discuss: Describe a time when someone was kind to you. How did it make you feel?
The text says kindness can mean standing up for someone. Why can that be difficult?
Plan one small act of kindness you could do at school this week. What will you do?

topic: World Diabetes Day and the Discovery of Insulin
zh: 世界糖尿病日：胰島素的發現

a.title: The Medicine That Saved Millions
text: November 14 is World Diabetes Day. Diabetes is an illness where there is too much sugar in the blood.
Our bodies need insulin to use sugar for energy. Some people's bodies cannot make enough insulin.
Long ago, children with this kind of diabetes did not live long.
In 1921, two scientists in Canada, Frederick Banting and Charles Best, found a way to make insulin as a medicine.
In 1922, a sick boy of 14 got the first shots. He got better! Banting was born on November 14, so the day is in his honour.
Today, millions of people use insulin. Healthy food and exercise also help people stay well.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: Diabetes and the discovery of insulin
The life of Frederick Banting
Why sugar is bad for children
How to exercise to stay healthy
q.why: 全文講糖尿病與胰島素；其他是細節。

q.q: What is diabetes?
opts: An illness caused by eating too little sugar
An illness where there is too much sugar in the blood
An illness that only children get
A medicine made from sugar
q.why: 第一段：too much sugar in the blood。

q.q: Why is World Diabetes Day on November 14?
opts: It is the day insulin was discovered
It is the day the first patient got better
It is the day the medicine was sold
It is Banting's birthday
q.why: 第五段：Banting was born on November 14。

q.q: In the text, “illness” means ___.
opts: a kind of medicine
a healthy habit
a sickness
a scientist
q.why: illness = 疾病。

q.q: Why was insulin such an important discovery?
opts: Before it, children with this kind of diabetes did not live long
It made sugar cheaper for everyone
It cured diabetes forever
It replaced healthy food and exercise
q.why: 第三段：children … did not live long——胰島素救了他們。

q.q: Your friend says, “If there is insulin, I don't need to care about healthy food.” What does the text suggest?
opts: He is right; insulin solves everything
Only adults need healthy food
Exercise is more important than insulin for everyone
Healthy food and exercise also help people stay well
q.why: 最後一段：Healthy food and exercise also help people stay well。

gt.en: Diabetes is an illness where there is too much sugar in the blood.
gt.zh: 糖尿病是一種血液中糖分太多的疾病。

gt.en: Our bodies need insulin to use sugar for energy.
gt.zh: 我們的身體需要胰島素，才能把糖變成能量來用。

gt.en: Healthy food and exercise also help people stay well.
gt.zh: 健康的飲食和運動也能幫助人們保持健康。

b.title: A Discovery That Changed a Death Sentence
text: World Diabetes Day is held each year on November 14, the birthday of Frederick Banting, the Canadian doctor who helped discover insulin.

Diabetes affects how the body controls blood sugar. In type 1 diabetes, the body cannot produce insulin, the hormone that lets cells absorb sugar. In the more common type 2, the body does not use insulin properly.
Before the 1920s, a diagnosis of type 1 diabetes was essentially a death sentence, especially for children.

In 1921, at the University of Toronto, Banting and his young assistant Charles Best managed to extract insulin. In January 1922, a 14-year-old boy named Leonard Thompson became the first person to receive an injection, and his condition dramatically improved.
Banting shared the 1923 Nobel Prize in Medicine. Remarkably, the discoverers sold the patent to the university for just one dollar each, hoping the medicine would be affordable.
Today more than half a billion adults live with diabetes. Doctors stress that regular exercise and a healthy diet can lower the risk of type 2.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Banting and Best sold the insulin patent for one dollar each.
The discovery of insulin turned a deadly illness into a treatable one, and diabetes remains a major health issue today.
Type 2 diabetes is more common than type 1.
Leonard Thompson was the first person to receive insulin.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文；其他是細節。

q.q: What is the difference between type 1 and type 2 diabetes?
opts: Type 1 affects only adults; type 2 affects only children
Type 1 is caused by sugar; type 2 is caused by insulin
In type 1 the body cannot produce insulin; in type 2 it does not use insulin properly
Type 1 can be cured; type 2 cannot
q.why: 第二段說明兩型差異。

q.q: How much did the discoverers sell the patent for?
opts: One dollar each
One thousand dollars each
Nothing; they gave it away
Enough to build a hospital
q.why: 第五段：for just one dollar each。

q.q: In paragraph 3, a “diagnosis” is ___.
opts: a treatment for an illness
a test of a new medicine
a patient's recovery
a doctor's identification of an illness
q.why: diagnosis = 診斷。

q.q: Why did the discoverers sell the patent so cheaply?
opts: They wanted the medicine to be affordable for patients
They were not sure the medicine would work
The university paid them in other ways
They wanted to avoid paying taxes
q.why: 第五段：hoping the medicine would be affordable。

q.q: A medicine company wants to sell a new life-saving drug at a very high price. Which argument from the text could be used AGAINST this?
opts: Insulin was discovered at a university
Banting won the Nobel Prize
Insulin's discoverers sold their patent cheaply so patients could afford it
Exercise lowers the risk of type 2 diabetes
q.why: 以一美元出售專利、讓藥物負擔得起的例子，可用來反對高價。

tr.en: In type 1 diabetes, the body cannot produce insulin, the hormone that lets cells absorb sugar.
tr.zh: 在第一型糖尿病中，身體無法製造胰島素——一種讓細胞能吸收糖分的荷爾蒙。

tr.en: Before the 1920s, a diagnosis of type 1 diabetes was essentially a death sentence, especially for children.
tr.zh: 在 1920 年代以前，被診斷出第一型糖尿病幾乎等於被判了死刑，對孩子來說尤其如此。

tr.en: In 1921, at the University of Toronto, Banting and his young assistant Charles Best managed to extract insulin.
tr.zh: 1921 年，在多倫多大學，班廷和他年輕的助手查爾斯・貝斯特成功地提取出胰島素。

c.title: From Death Sentence to Daily Routine
text: Few medical breakthroughs have been as immediate in their effect as insulin. Before 1922, children diagnosed with what is now called type 1 diabetes faced a grim prognosis; the most doctors could offer was a starvation diet that prolonged life by months.

The turning point came at the University of Toronto, where the surgeon Frederick Banting, born on November 14, 1891, and the student Charles Best extracted the hormone from animal pancreases in 1921. Within weeks of the first injections, emaciated patients regained their strength.

The story contains a striking gesture of idealism. Banting and his colleagues sold the patent to the university for a nominal one dollar each, wanting the treatment to belong to humanity rather than to profit.

A century later that ideal sits uneasily with reality. In some countries insulin remains expensive enough that patients ration it, and the global prevalence of diabetes, now exceeding half a billion adults, is rising fastest where healthcare is weakest.
World Diabetes Day, observed on Banting's birthday, therefore honours a discovery while posing an unfinished question: whether a cure that exists can reach everyone who needs it.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Insulin was a life-saving breakthrough, but its founders' ideal of access for all is still unfulfilled.
Thanks to insulin, diabetes is no longer a serious problem.
Banting was the most important scientist of the twentieth century.
Diabetes is rising mainly because of unhealthy diets.
q.why: 主旨：胰島素救命，但人人可得的理想仍未實現。

q.q: In paragraph 3, a “nominal” price is ___.
opts: fair and reasonable
very small, almost symbolic
set by the government
higher than expected
q.why: nominal = 象徵性的。

q.q: What does it mean that some patients “ration” insulin?
opts: They store it carefully in the fridge
They share it with family members
They take it only at certain times of day
They use less than they need because it is too expensive
q.why: 第四段：因為太貴，病人只好省著用。

q.q: How does the writer view the gap between the discoverers' ideal and today's reality?
opts: Optimistic that it is already solved
Indifferent
Concerned and critical
Amused
q.why: sits uneasily with reality——憂心且帶批判。

q.q: What does the final sentence add?
opts: A summary of how insulin works
An unfinished question about access to the cure
A call to give Banting more credit
A prediction that diabetes will disappear
q.why: 結尾提出未解問題：治療能否送到每個需要的人。

q.q: Which statistic would BEST support the writer's concern in paragraph 4?
opts: The year insulin was first used
The number of Nobel Prizes won by Canadians
The number of patients who skip insulin doses because of cost
The amount of sugar in a can of soda
q.why: 第四段的擔憂是價格讓病人省著用；因費用而減量的病人數最能支持。

discuss: Banting sold the patent for one dollar. Should important medicines be cheap for everyone? Why or why not?
What healthy habits can students build to lower the risk of illnesses like type 2 diabetes?
How much sugar do you think you eat in a day? Where does most of it come from?

zh: 潘朵拉的盒子

a.title: Don't Open It!
text: This is a story from ancient Greece. Long ago, a man named Prometheus took fire from the gods and gave it to people.
Zeus, the king of the gods, was very angry. He made the first woman, Pandora, and sent her to Earth.
The gods gave Pandora a jar and said, “Never open it.”
But Pandora was curious. One day, she opened the jar a little.
Out flew sickness, sadness, and all the troubles of the world! She quickly closed it, but only one thing was left inside: hope.
Today, people say “open Pandora's box” when one small action causes many problems.

q.q: What is this story mainly about?
opts: How Prometheus took fire from the gods
Why Zeus was the king of the gods
How Pandora opened a jar and let troubles into the world
Why hope is the most important thing
q.why: 故事主線是潘朵拉打開罐子；其他是背景或細節。

q.q: Why was Zeus angry?
opts: Pandora opened the jar without asking
People forgot to thank the gods
Pandora refused to go to Earth
Prometheus took fire from the gods and gave it to people
q.why: 第一、二段：Prometheus took fire from the gods。

q.q: What was left inside the jar?
opts: Hope
Sickness
Sadness
Fire
q.why: 第五段：only one thing was left inside: hope。

q.q: In the text, “curious” means ___.
opts: not caring about anything
wanting to know about something
afraid of something
angry about something
q.why: curious = 好奇的。

q.q: What does “open Pandora's box” mean today?
opts: To find something very valuable
To give someone a present
To do something small that causes many problems
To keep a secret safely
q.why: 最後一段：one small action causes many problems。

q.q: Which situation is the BEST example of “opening Pandora's box”?
opts: Tom opens a birthday present and is very happy
Tom shares one secret, and soon many rumours and fights start
Tom finds his lost keys in a box
Tom closes the window before it rains
q.why: 一個小舉動引發一連串問題——分享祕密後謠言和爭吵接連發生。

gt.en: This is a story from ancient Greece.
gt.zh: 這是一個來自古希臘的故事。

gt.en: Zeus, the king of the gods, was very angry.
gt.zh: 眾神之王宙斯非常生氣。

gt.en: The gods gave Pandora a jar and said, “Never open it.”
gt.zh: 眾神給了潘朵拉一個罐子，並說：「永遠不要打開它。」

gt.en: One day, she opened the jar a little.
gt.zh: 有一天，她把罐子打開了一點點。

b.title: The Jar That Changed the World
text: In Greek mythology, the story of Pandora explains how suffering entered human life. It was first written down by the poet Hesiod around 700 BC.

When the Titan Prometheus stole fire from the gods and gave it to humans, Zeus decided to punish humankind. He ordered Hephaestus, the god of craftsmen, to shape the first woman, Pandora, out of clay.
Each god gave her a gift — beauty, charm, skill — and Zeus gave her a sealed jar, warning that it must never be opened. Pandora was sent to marry Epimetheus, Prometheus's less careful brother.
Overcome by curiosity, Pandora lifted the lid. Out rushed disease, hard work, sorrow and countless other evils, which spread across the world. Only Hope remained trapped beneath the rim.
Interestingly, the original story describes a large storage jar, not a box. The word 'box' comes from a translation mistake made by a scholar in the 1500s.
Today the phrase 'opening Pandora's box' describes an action that releases a series of unexpected problems.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Hephaestus made the first woman, Pandora, out of clay.
The word 'box' came from a translation mistake in the 1500s.
The Pandora myth explains how suffering came into the world, and its name lives on in a common phrase.
Zeus punished Prometheus for stealing fire.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文；其他是細節。

q.q: Who shaped Pandora out of clay?
opts: Prometheus
Hephaestus
Zeus
Epimetheus
q.why: 第二段：He ordered Hephaestus … to shape the first woman。

q.q: Why do we say 'box' instead of 'jar'?
opts: Because Hesiod wrote 'box' in his poem
Because the jar was later replaced by a box
Because Zeus called it a box
Because of a translation mistake in the 1500s
q.why: 第五段：a translation mistake made by a scholar in the 1500s。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “sealed” means ___.
opts: tightly closed
beautifully decorated
very heavy
already empty
q.why: sealed = 密封的。

q.q: Why was Pandora sent to Epimetheus instead of Prometheus?
opts: He was the one who stole fire
He was the less careful brother, more likely to accept the gift
He had asked Zeus for a wife
He was the strongest god
q.why: 第三段：Prometheus's less careful brother——比較容易上當。

q.q: A website says: “In the ancient Greek story, Pandora opened a box.” Based on the text, how accurate is this?
opts: Partly wrong — the original story describes a large jar, not a box
Completely correct
Completely wrong — Pandora never opened anything
Partly wrong — it was Epimetheus who opened it
q.why: 第五段：原文是大儲物罐，「盒子」是 1500 年代的翻譯錯誤。

tr.en: In Greek mythology, the story of Pandora explains how suffering entered human life.
tr.zh: 在希臘神話中，潘朵拉的故事解釋了苦難是如何進入人類生活的。

tr.en: When the Titan Prometheus stole fire from the gods and gave it to humans, Zeus decided to punish humankind.
tr.zh: 當泰坦神普羅米修斯從眾神那裡偷走火、交給人類時，宙斯決定懲罰人類。

tr.en: Today the phrase 'opening Pandora's box' describes an action that releases a series of unexpected problems.
tr.zh: 今天，「打開潘朵拉的盒子」這個片語，用來形容一個引發一連串意外問題的行為。

c.title: The Puzzle of Hope
text: The tale of Pandora, preserved in the poems of Hesiod from around 700 BC, is usually told as a simple warning against curiosity. Read closely, it is stranger and more troubling than that.

Zeus, enraged that Prometheus had given fire to humanity, devised a punishment disguised as a gift: Pandora, fashioned from clay by Hephaestus and adorned by every god. With her came a sealed jar, a pithos for storing grain or oil, which centuries later a Renaissance translator rendered as a 'box', fixing the image in European imagination.
When Pandora lifted the lid, disease, toil and grief escaped into a world that had previously known none of them. Only Elpis, usually translated as Hope, stayed inside.

That detail has puzzled readers ever since. Is hope a blessing preserved for humanity, or simply one more evil, a deceptive expectation that prolongs our suffering? The text never settles the question.

Perhaps that ambiguity is the myth's enduring power: it does not tell us whether to cling to hope or distrust it, only that, among all the troubles of the world, it is the one that remains closest at hand.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: The myth's only lesson is that curiosity is dangerous.
The Pandora myth is more than a warning about curiosity; its unresolved meaning of hope gives it lasting power.
Hope was clearly the worst evil in the jar.
The myth is important mainly because of the translation mistake.
q.why: 主旨：不只警告好奇心，「希望」意義未定才是它歷久不衰的力量。

q.q: In paragraph 5, “ambiguity” means ___.
opts: the quality of having more than one possible meaning
a clear and simple lesson
a strong feeling of hope
an old translation
q.why: ambiguity = 模稜兩可。

q.q: Why have readers been puzzled that Hope stayed in the jar?
opts: Hesiod forgot to explain why the jar was closed
Hope escaped in later versions of the story
The jar was too small for hope to escape
It is unclear whether hope is a blessing kept for humans or another evil
q.why: 第四段：Is hope a blessing … or simply one more evil?

q.q: How does the writer approach the myth?
opts: Critically, calling it a sexist story
Simply, retelling it for children
Thoughtfully, exploring its open questions
Doubtfully, questioning whether it is really Greek
q.why: 作者細讀並探討開放問題。

q.q: What role does paragraph 2's note about the 'box' play?
opts: It explains how a translation shaped the familiar image of the story
It introduces the main argument about hope
It describes Prometheus's punishment
It gives the story's moral
q.why: 第二段說明翻譯如何塑造了「盒子」的印象。

q.q: Which real-life example best illustrates hope as a “deceptive expectation that prolongs our suffering”?
opts: Someone studies hard, hoping to pass an exam
A doctor hopes a new treatment will help patients
Someone keeps buying lottery tickets, sure that next time they will win
A team practises, hoping to win next season
q.why: 沒有依據、反覆期待中獎而持續花錢，最符合「延長痛苦的欺騙性期待」。

discuss: Is curiosity a good thing or a dangerous thing? Give an example.
Why do you think Hope stayed in the jar? Is hope a gift or a problem?
Can you think of a real-life situation where one small action 'opened Pandora's box'?

zh: 一戰停戰日：為什麼人們戴上罌粟花？

a.title: The Day the Guns Stopped
text: More than 100 years ago, there was a terrible war in Europe. It was called the First World War.
Millions of soldiers died. Many families lost fathers, sons, and brothers.
On November 11, 1918, at 11 o'clock in the morning, the fighting finally stopped.
Today, people in many countries remember this day. At 11 o'clock, they stand quietly for two minutes.
Many people wear a red poppy flower. Poppies grew on the fields where soldiers fought.
The poppy helps us remember the people who died, and it reminds us that peace is precious.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: Why red poppies grow on battlefields
The end of the First World War and how people remember it
How millions of soldiers died in Europe
Why people stand quietly at 11 o'clock
q.why: 全文講一戰結束與紀念方式；其他是細節。

q.q: When did the fighting stop?
opts: At midnight on November 11, 1918
At 11 o'clock on November 11, 1919
At 11 o'clock on November 11, 1918
At 11 o'clock on November 1, 1918
q.why: 第三段：On November 11, 1918, at 11 o'clock。

q.q: What do people do at 11 o'clock on this day?
opts: They stand quietly for two minutes
They stand quietly for eleven minutes
They plant red poppies
They ring bells for one hour
q.why: 第四段：they stand quietly for two minutes。

q.q: In the text, “peace” means ___.
opts: a time to remember soldiers
a kind of red flower
a quiet place
a time without war
q.why: peace = 和平。

q.q: Why is the poppy used to remember soldiers?
opts: Poppies grew on the fields where soldiers fought
Poppies were the soldiers' favourite flower
Poppies are red like the national flags
Soldiers planted poppies before the war
q.why: 第五段：Poppies grew on the fields where soldiers fought。

q.q: Your school wants to remember the First World War on November 11. Which activity fits the text best?
opts: A big party with music and fireworks
A sports day with prizes for winners
A sale of war toys
A two-minute silence at 11 o'clock and wearing paper poppies
q.why: 文中的紀念方式是十一點默哀兩分鐘、戴罌粟花。

gt.en: More than 100 years ago, there was a terrible war in Europe.
gt.zh: 一百多年前，歐洲發生了一場可怕的戰爭。

gt.en: On November 11, 1918, at 11 o'clock in the morning, the fighting finally stopped.
gt.zh: 1918 年 11 月 11 日早上十一點，戰鬥終於停止了。

gt.en: Today, people in many countries remember this day.
gt.zh: 今天，許多國家的人都會紀念這一天。

gt.en: Many people wear a red poppy flower.
gt.zh: 許多人會戴上一朵紅色的罌粟花。

b.title: The Eleventh Hour of the Eleventh Day
text: At 11 a.m. on November 11, 1918, the guns of the First World War fell silent. Hours earlier, leaders had signed an armistice — an agreement to stop fighting — in a railway carriage in a forest near Compiègne, France.
The war had lasted more than four years and killed around nine million soldiers, along with millions of civilians.
Each year, many countries mark the anniversary. In Britain and the Commonwealth it is called Remembrance Day, in the United States Veterans Day, and in France and Belgium Armistice Day.
At 11 o'clock, many people observe two minutes of silence, a tradition that began in 1919.

The red poppy became the symbol of remembrance because poppies bloomed across the churned-up battlefields of Flanders. A Canadian doctor, John McCrae, wrote a famous poem about them in 1915, and the flower was soon adopted to honour the dead.
The war was once called 'the war to end all wars'. Sadly, it did not — which is one reason people still pause to remember.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: The armistice was signed in a railway carriage near Compiègne.
The First World War killed around nine million soldiers.
The end of the First World War on 11 November 1918 is still remembered with silence and poppies.
John McCrae wrote a famous poem about poppies.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文；其他是細節。

q.q: Where was the armistice signed?
opts: In a church in Flanders, Belgium
In a palace in London
In a hospital near the front line
In a railway carriage in a forest near Compiègne, France
q.why: 第一段：in a railway carriage in a forest near Compiègne。

q.q: What is the day called in the United States?
opts: Remembrance Day
Veterans Day
Armistice Day
Memorial Day
q.why: 第三段：in the United States Veterans Day。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “civilians” are ___.
opts: people who are not soldiers
soldiers who were injured
leaders who signed the armistice
doctors who helped soldiers
q.why: civilians = 平民。

q.q: Why does the writer say 'sadly, it did not'?
opts: Because more wars happened after it, so it did not end all wars
Because the armistice was broken the next day
Because people stopped remembering the war
Because poppies stopped growing in Flanders
q.why: 被稱為終結所有戰爭的戰爭，可惜之後仍有戰爭。

q.q: A student says: “Remembrance Day is about celebrating who won the war.” Based on the text, what is the best response?
opts: Yes, it celebrates the victory of the winning countries
It is mainly about the history of poppies
It is a holiday only for soldiers
It is mainly about remembering those who died and the cost of war
q.why: 文中的默哀與罌粟花都是為了紀念逝者，而非慶祝勝利。

tr.en: Hours earlier, leaders had signed an armistice — an agreement to stop fighting — in a railway carriage in a forest near Compiègne, France.
tr.zh: 幾個小時前，領導人們在法國貢比涅附近森林裡的一節火車車廂中，簽署了停戰協定——一份停止戰鬥的協議。

tr.en: The war had lasted more than four years and killed around nine million soldiers, along with millions of civilians.
tr.zh: 這場戰爭持續了四年多，奪走了大約九百萬名士兵的性命，還有數百萬名平民。

tr.en: In Britain and the Commonwealth it is called Remembrance Day, in the United States Veterans Day, and in France and Belgium Armistice Day.
tr.zh: 在英國和大英國協，它叫做陣亡將士紀念日；在美國叫做退伍軍人節；在法國和比利時則叫做停戰紀念日。

c.title: Remembering at the Eleventh Hour
text: There is a deliberate symmetry to the moment the First World War ended: the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month of 1918. The armistice had been signed at dawn in a railway carriage near Compiègne, yet fighting continued until the appointed hour, and soldiers were still dying in the final minutes of the war.
The conflict had killed roughly nine million combatants and devastated a generation, and the scale of loss demanded new forms of public mourning.

The two minutes' silence, first observed in 1919, turned private grief into a shared national act. The red poppy, drawn from the flowers that bloomed on the churned soil of Flanders and immortalised in John McCrae's poem, gave remembrance a simple, wearable form.

These rituals were never uncontroversial. Some feared they glorified sacrifice, while others insisted they were acts of mourning, not celebration — a debate that continues whenever symbols of remembrance are politicised.

More than a century on, the ceremonies endure partly because the hope attached to them, that this would be the war to end all wars, proved so tragically mistaken. To remember, in this sense, is not to admire war but to keep alive an argument for peace.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: The ceremonies mainly celebrate military victory.
The rituals of remembrance endure as a way to mourn and to keep alive an argument for peace, not to admire war.
The poppy is the most important symbol of the twentieth century.
The war ended the moment the armistice was signed at dawn.
q.why: 主旨：紀念儀式是為了哀悼與延續和平的主張。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “immortalised” means ___.
opts: made famous and remembered forever
made sad and serious
made political
made simple
q.why: immortalised = 使不朽。

q.q: What does the writer suggest by noting soldiers died in the final minutes?
opts: The armistice was signed too early
Soldiers did not believe the war was over
Leaders wanted the war to continue
Waiting for a symbolic hour had a real human cost
q.why: 為了等象徵性的時刻，最後幾分鐘仍有人喪命。

q.q: How does the writer present the debate over remembrance rituals?
opts: As a clear win for the critics
As an argument that should be ignored
Even-handedly, describing both concerns and defences
Only from the side of the defenders
q.why: 第四段同時呈現兩方看法。

q.q: How does the final paragraph connect to the phrase 'the war to end all wars'?
opts: It says the phrase was correct
It says the ceremonies endure partly because that hope proved tragically wrong
It explains who first used the phrase
It argues the phrase should be forgotten
q.why: 結尾：the hope … proved so tragically mistaken。

q.q: A politician uses the poppy in an advertisement asking for more military spending. Based on paragraph 4, why might some people object?
opts: They think poppies are too expensive
They believe the war never happened
They feel remembrance symbols should not be politicised to glorify war
They think advertisements should not use flowers
q.why: 第四段：有人擔心紀念象徵被政治化、美化犧牲。

discuss: Why do you think people still remember a war that ended more than 100 years ago?
How are wars or historical tragedies remembered in Taiwan? Compare with the poppy and two minutes' silence.
Some say remembrance days can glorify war; others say they honour the dead and support peace. What do you think?

zh: 國際寬容日：不一樣也沒關係

a.title: Different Is OK
text: November 16 is the International Day for Tolerance. Tolerance means accepting people who are different from you.
People are different in many ways. They speak different languages, eat different food, and believe different things.
Tolerance does not mean you must agree with everyone. It means you treat other people with respect.
UNESCO, part of the United Nations, started this day in 1995.
At school, tolerance can be simple. You can listen to a new classmate, try a new food, or stop a joke that hurts someone.
When people respect each other, schools and cities become safer and happier.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How to learn a new language

b.title: Living Together With Our Differences
text: Every year on November 16, UNESCO marks the International Day for Tolerance. The date recalls a declaration on tolerance that its members adopted in 1995, which the United Nations had named the Year for Tolerance.
The declaration describes tolerance as respect and appreciation for the rich diversity of the world's cultures and ways of being human.
Importantly, tolerance is not the same as giving up your own beliefs. People can disagree strongly and still treat each other fairly, without insults or violence.
Intolerance often grows from ignorance and fear. When people know little about a group, rumours and stereotypes fill the gap, and those can turn into discrimination.
That is why education is seen as the most effective way to prevent intolerance. Learning other people's stories, languages and histories makes differences feel less threatening.
Online life adds a new challenge: angry posts spread quickly, so pausing before sharing has become a small but real act of tolerance.

c.title: The Hard Virtue
text: Tolerance is often mistaken for a soft virtue, a polite shrug in the face of difference. The International Day for Tolerance, held on November 16 to recall UNESCO's 1995 declaration, insists on something more demanding.

Genuine tolerance begins where comfort ends. It is easy to accept people whose habits are merely unfamiliar; it is harder to extend fairness to those whose convictions we find mistaken, even offensive.

Crucially, tolerance is not relativism. It does not require us to pretend that all ideas are equally sound. It requires that we argue with ideas while respecting the dignity and rights of the people who hold them.
Nor is it limitless. A society that tolerates the persecution of minorities in the name of open-mindedness ends up protecting the intolerant at the expense of everyone else.

Education remains the most reliable defence, because prejudice thrives where knowledge is thin. Yet the digital age, which rewards outrage with attention, makes the old discipline of listening before judging more valuable than ever.

a.title: A Short Way Across the World

b.title: The Canal That Shrank the World
text: When the Suez Canal opened on November 17, 1869, it changed the map of world trade. For the first time, ships could sail directly between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea instead of making the long, dangerous voyage around the southern tip of Africa.

The project was led by the French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps, but the digging was done by tens of thousands of Egyptian workers, many of them forced to work in harsh conditions. Large numbers died from disease and exhaustion.

The canal quickly became one of the world's most valuable routes. Control over it became a source of conflict, and in 1956 Egypt's president, Gamal Abdel Nasser, nationalised it, triggering an international crisis.
Today the canal has been widened and deepened many times. In normal years, roughly a tenth of global trade passes through it.

Its importance became clear in March 2021, when a giant container ship, the Ever Given, blocked it for six days. Hundreds of vessels were trapped in a queue, and the delay disrupted supply chains around the world.

c.title: A Narrow Channel, A Wide World
text: Few engineering works have compressed the planet as dramatically as the Suez Canal. Opened on November 17, 1869, it spared ships the perilous voyage around Africa and cut thousands of kilometres from the journey between Europe and Asia.

The celebrations, attended by European royalty, obscured an uncomfortable truth. The canal was conceived by the French entrepreneur Ferdinand de Lesseps, but it was dug largely by Egyptian labourers, tens of thousands of them conscripted, many of whom perished. Egypt soon fell into debt, and the canal's profits flowed mostly abroad.

That history explains why control of the waterway became a matter of national pride. When Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised it in 1956, Britain, France and Israel intervened militarily, only to withdraw under international pressure, a turning point in the decline of European empires.
The canal's strategic weight has not faded. In March 2021 a single grounded container ship, the Ever Given, halted traffic for six days and exposed how fragile global supply chains had become.
The lesson is double-edged: shortcuts create enormous efficiency, but concentrating so much of the world's trade in one narrow channel also concentrates risk.

a.title: The Mouse Who Whistled

b.title: How Sound Made a Star
text: On November 18, 1928, audiences at the Colony Theatre in New York watched a seven-minute cartoon called Steamboat Willie. It is remembered as the debut of Mickey Mouse, the character who would build an entertainment empire.

Mickey had actually appeared in earlier silent films that had not yet been released. What made Steamboat Willie a sensation was sound: music, whistles and noises were carefully synchronised with the action on screen.
Walt Disney voiced Mickey himself, while his partner Ub Iwerks led the animation. Audiences were delighted, and studios quickly realised that sound cartoons were the future.
Nearly a century later, the film made headlines again. In the United States, its copyright expired on January 1, 2024, so the original 1928 version of Mickey entered the public domain.
That does not mean anyone can use Mickey freely. Later versions of the character are still protected, and Disney keeps Mickey as a trademark, so people cannot pretend their products come from Disney.

c.title: A Mouse, a Whistle and the Public Domain
text: On November 18, 1928, a seven-minute cartoon premiered in New York and quietly redrew the boundaries of popular entertainment. Steamboat Willie was not technically Mickey Mouse's first film, but it was the first to be released, and its tightly synchronised soundtrack turned a cheerful, whistling rodent into a phenomenon.

Its genius was technical as much as artistic. Walt Disney, who voiced the character himself, and his animator Ub Iwerks timed every gesture to music and sound effects, persuading audiences that the drawings were genuinely making noise.

From that modest premiere grew one of the most valuable brands in history, and with it a long political struggle over how long creative works should remain private property. American copyright terms were extended more than once in the twentieth century, extensions critics nicknamed the 'Mickey Mouse Protection Act'.
Yet time eventually won. On January 1, 2024, the original Steamboat Willie entered the US public domain, free for artists and teachers to reuse and reimagine.

The limits matter. Later versions remain protected, and trademark law still prevents anyone from implying a product is made by Disney. The episode illustrates the bargain at copyright's heart: creators deserve rewards, but culture also needs a common store of works that everyone can build upon.

b.title: The Invention That Saves Millions of Lives
text: World Toilet Day, held every November 19, began in 2001 when the Singaporean campaigner Jack Sim founded the World Toilet Organization. In 2013 the United Nations made it an official observance.

The topic makes some people giggle, but the numbers are sobering. According to UN figures, around 3.5 billion people still lack safely managed sanitation, and hundreds of millions have no toilet at all.

When human waste is not safely contained, it contaminates rivers, fields and drinking water. That spreads diseases such as cholera and diarrhoea, which remain major causes of death for young children in poorer countries.
Toilets also affect education and safety. Girls are more likely to miss school if there are no private, hygienic facilities, and women who must go outside at night can face danger.
Experts stress that building toilets is only the first step. Waste must also be collected and treated, or the problem simply moves downstream.

Toilets are a funny subject that should not be discussed.

q.q: About how many people lack safely managed sanitation?

Everyone in poorer countries
Around 3.5 billion
q.why: 第二段：around 3.5 billion people。

Cholera and diarrhoea
Diabetes and cancer
Polio and measles
q.why: 第三段：cholera and diarrhoea。

serious and making you think carefully

tr.en: Toilets also affect education and safety.
tr.zh: 廁所也影響教育和安全。

tr.zh: 專家強調，蓋廁所只是第一步。

c.title: The Unglamorous Revolution
text: Few inventions are less celebrated or more consequential than the humble toilet. World Toilet Day, observed each November 19 and adopted by the United Nations in 2013, exists precisely because the subject is so easy to laugh off.

The scale of the shortfall is striking. Roughly 3.5 billion people lack safely managed sanitation, and hundreds of millions still have no facility at all. Where waste is not contained and treated, it seeps into water supplies and fuels diseases that kill hundreds of thousands of young children every year.

Historians of public health often argue that sanitation saved more lives than almost any medical breakthrough. The sewers built in nineteenth-century cities, prompted by deadly cholera outbreaks, transformed life expectancy long before modern drugs existed.
The consequences extend beyond disease. Without private, safe facilities, girls drop out of school and women face harassment; dignity itself is at stake.

Yet the solution is not merely to install more toilets. Without systems to collect and treat waste, sanitation simply relocates the problem. The real revolution is unglamorous infrastructure, quietly maintained.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Toilets are a minor issue compared with medicine.
Nineteenth-century sewers caused cholera.
Sanitation is a hugely important but overlooked foundation of health, education and dignity — and it requires whole systems, not just toilets.
Installing more toilets is the complete solution.
q.why: 主旨：衛生設施影響重大卻被忽視，而且需要完整系統。

topic: Edwin Hubble and the Growing Universe
zh: 哈伯：發現宇宙正在變大的人

a.title: The Man Who Saw Other Galaxies
text: Edwin Hubble was born on November 20, 1889, in the United States. He became a famous astronomer.
An astronomer studies stars and space. Hubble used a very big telescope on a mountain in California.
Long ago, people thought our galaxy, the Milky Way, was the whole universe. Hubble showed that there are many other galaxies far away.
He also found that most galaxies are moving away from us. This means the universe is getting bigger!
Today, a space telescope has his name: the Hubble Space Telescope. It has taken amazing pictures since 1990.
Hubble's work changed how we see our place in space.

opts: The Hubble Space Telescope's pictures
Edwin Hubble and what he discovered about space
A mountain in California
How to become an astronomer

q.q: What did people think long ago?
opts: That galaxies were moving closer
That telescopes were not useful
That the Milky Way was the whole universe
That the universe was getting bigger
q.why: 第三段：people thought our galaxy … was the whole universe。

q.q: When did the Hubble Space Telescope start taking pictures?
q.why: 第五段：It has taken amazing pictures since 1990。

q.q: In the text, an “astronomer” is a person who ___.
opts: builds mountains
takes photos of people
drives a spaceship
studies stars and space

q.q: Why does the text say the universe is getting bigger?
opts: Because most galaxies are moving away from us
Because the telescope is very big
Because there are more stars every year
Because Hubble was born in 1889
q.why: 第四段：most galaxies are moving away from us. This means the universe is getting bigger!

gt.zh: 他也發現大部分星系正在遠離我們。

gt.zh: 哈伯的研究改變了我們看待自己在宇宙中位置的方式。

b.title: Beyond the Milky Way
text: Edwin Hubble, born in Missouri on November 20, 1889, first studied law at Oxford before returning to his real passion: the stars.

In the early 1920s, astronomers were still arguing about whether fuzzy patches of light called nebulae were inside our galaxy or far beyond it. Using the giant Hooker telescope at Mount Wilson in California, Hubble measured special pulsing stars in the Andromeda nebula and showed that it was far too distant to belong to the Milky Way.
Andromeda was a separate galaxy, and suddenly the universe was vastly larger than anyone had imagined.

In 1929 Hubble published another landmark result: the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it appears to be moving away from us. This was strong evidence that the universe is expanding. The Belgian scientist Georges Lemaître had proposed a similar idea two years earlier, which is why the rule is now often called the Hubble–Lemaître law.
In 1990 NASA launched a space telescope in his honour, which continues his work above Earth's blurry atmosphere.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Hubble showed that other galaxies exist and that the universe is expanding.
Hubble studied law at Oxford.
Lemaître built the Hooker telescope.
The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1929.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：證明其他星系存在、宇宙在膨脹。

q.q: How did Hubble show Andromeda was outside the Milky Way?
opts: He travelled there
He read Lemaître's paper
He measured special pulsing stars and found it was too far away
He used the space telescope
q.why: 第二段：measured special pulsing stars … far too distant。

q.q: What did Hubble publish in 1929?
opts: That Andromeda is a nebula
That the universe is shrinking
That the Milky Way is the only galaxy
That farther galaxies seem to move away faster
q.why: 第四段：the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it appears to be moving away。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “expanding” means ___.
opts: getting colder
getting bigger
staying the same
turning around
q.why: expanding = 擴張、變大。

q.q: Why is the rule now often called the Hubble–Lemaître law?
opts: Because Lemaître built Hubble's telescope
Because they were brothers
Because NASA named it in 1990
Because Lemaître proposed a similar idea earlier
q.why: 第四段：Lemaître had proposed a similar idea two years earlier。

q.q: A website says: “Hubble alone came up with the idea that the universe is expanding.” Based on the text, is this fair?
opts: Not fully, because Lemaître proposed a similar idea two years earlier
Yes, nobody else studied it
Yes, because the telescope has his name
No, because Hubble studied law, not stars
q.why: 第四段：勒梅特早兩年提出類似想法。

tr.en: Andromeda was a separate galaxy, and suddenly the universe was vastly larger than anyone had imagined.
tr.zh: 仙女座是一個獨立的星系，宇宙一下子變得比任何人想像的都大得多。

tr.en: This was strong evidence that the universe is expanding.
tr.zh: 這是宇宙正在膨脹的有力證據。

tr.en: In 1990 NASA launched a space telescope in his honour, which continues his work above Earth's blurry atmosphere.
tr.zh: 1990 年，NASA 發射了一架以他命名的太空望遠鏡，在地球模糊的大氣層之上延續他的工作。

c.title: How Big Is Everything?
text: A century ago, the most basic question in astronomy, how big the universe is, had no agreed answer. Many astronomers believed the Milky Way contained everything; the faint spiral 'nebulae' scattered across the sky were assumed to be clouds within it.

Edwin Hubble, born on November 20, 1889, settled the dispute. In 1923, working with the great Hooker telescope at Mount Wilson, he identified a Cepheid variable, a star whose regular pulsing reveals its true brightness, in the Andromeda nebula. Comparing true and apparent brightness yielded a distance far beyond our galaxy's edge.
The implication was staggering: Andromeda was an 'island universe', and the cosmos contained countless such galaxies.

Six years later he went further, showing that galaxies recede at speeds proportional to their distance. The universe was not static but expanding, a conclusion the Belgian priest-physicist Georges Lemaître had already reached theoretically, which is why astronomers now speak of the Hubble–Lemaître law.

Hubble never won a Nobel Prize, which did not then recognise astronomy. Yet his findings demoted humanity twice, from the centre of a single galaxy to one corner of an expanding cosmos, and few scientific discoveries have so thoroughly rescaled our sense of home.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Hubble's main achievement was winning a Nobel Prize.
Lemaître proved that Andromeda is a cloud.
Hubble's discoveries showed a universe of countless galaxies that is expanding, dramatically changing humanity's sense of its place.
The Milky Way contains everything in the universe.
q.why: 主旨：無數星系＋宇宙膨脹，徹底改變人類的定位。

q.why: recede = 後退、遠離。

q.q: Why was the Cepheid variable star so useful?
opts: It was the brightest star in the sky
It was inside the Milky Way
It proved the universe is static
Its regular pulsing reveals its true brightness, which lets astronomers calculate distance
q.why: 第二段：its regular pulsing reveals its true brightness——比較真實與視亮度可推算距離。

q.q: How does the writer view Hubble's lack of a Nobel Prize?
opts: As a technicality that does not reduce the importance of his discoveries
As proof his work was minor
As unfair to Lemaître
As a mistake by NASA
q.why: 第五段：諾貝爾獎當時不包含天文學，但他的發現依然極重要（Yet …）。

q.q: What does the phrase “demoted humanity twice” refer to?

Two arguments with Lemaître
Two discoveries that each made humans' place in the universe seem smaller
q.why: 結尾：從單一星系的中心，降為膨脹宇宙中的一角。

q.q: Which piece of evidence was MOST important for proving Andromeda is outside the Milky Way?

The distance calculated from a Cepheid star's true and apparent brightness

q.why: 第二段：用造父變星的真實與視亮度算出距離，才證明它在銀河系之外。

a.title: Fish for Tomorrow
text: November 21 is World Fisheries Day. It reminds us to take care of the fish in our seas, rivers and lakes.
Fish are an important food for billions of people. Millions of people also work as fishers.
But some people catch too many fish. Then there are not enough young fish to grow up and lay eggs. This is called overfishing.
Today, more than one third of the world's fish groups are overfished.
Some fish now come from fish farms. Farms can help, but they must be clean and careful too.

b.title: Can the Oceans Keep Feeding Us?
text: World Fisheries Day, celebrated on November 21, was started in 1997 by fishing communities who met in New Delhi to call for responsible fishing around the world.
Fish and seafood are a major source of protein for billions of people, and fishing supports the jobs of tens of millions more, from small boats to large factory ships.

However, the oceans are under pressure. According to the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization, more than a third of the world's fish stocks are now overfished, meaning they are caught faster than they can reproduce.
Illegal fishing, harmful methods that destroy the seabed, and bycatch, the accidental capture of dolphins, turtles and sharks, make the problem worse.
Fish farming, or aquaculture, now produces more than half of the seafood we eat. It can reduce pressure on wild fish, but poorly managed farms can pollute coastal waters.
Experts say the solution includes catch limits, protected marine areas and better tracking of where fish come from.

Fish feed and employ billions, but overfishing threatens the oceans, so responsible fishing is needed.
Aquaculture has completely solved overfishing.
Dolphins and turtles are the main food for humans.

q.q: What does “overfished” mean in the text?
opts: Fish are caught faster than they can reproduce
Too many fish farms
Fish are too big
Fish are only caught by small boats

None
More than half

tr.zh: 然而，海洋正承受壓力。

c.title: The Tragedy of the Open Sea
text: The ocean once seemed inexhaustible. Today, World Fisheries Day, marked each November 21 since 1997, serves as an annual reminder that it is not.

According to the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization, more than a third of assessed fish stocks are overfished, harvested faster than they can replenish themselves. The causes are partly technological: sonar, vast nets and subsidised fleets allow fishers to locate and remove fish with an efficiency earlier generations could not imagine.

Economists describe the dynamic as a 'tragedy of the commons'. Because no single fisher owns the sea, each has an incentive to catch as much as possible before others do, even though restraint would leave everyone better off.

Aquaculture has eased some pressure and now supplies most of the seafood humans eat, but it brings its own costs, including coastal pollution and, for some species, a reliance on wild fish ground into feed.

The most promising answers are institutional rather than technical: enforceable quotas, marine reserves where stocks can recover, and traceability that lets consumers reward responsible fleets. The sea can recover remarkably quickly, but only if people agree to share it.

q.why: 最後一段：enforceable quotas, marine reserves … traceability。

a.title: Be Careful What You Wish For
text: Long ago, in a Greek story, there was a king named Midas. He loved gold more than anything.
One day, Midas helped a friend of the god Dionysus. To thank him, the god gave Midas one wish.
Midas said, 'I wish that everything I touch turns into gold!' His wish came true.
At first he was very happy. He touched a stone, a flower and a chair, and they all became gold.
But then he tried to eat. His bread and water turned into gold too! Midas was hungry and afraid.
He asked the god to take the gift back. Midas learned that some things are worth more than gold.

q.q: What is this story mainly about?

A king whose golden wish caused trouble
A friend of the god Dionysus
Why gold is beautiful

q.q: Why did the god give Midas a wish?

Because Midas was hungry
Because Midas helped the god's friend
Because Midas was a god

His food tasted better
He became a god

b.title: The Curse of the Golden Touch
text: In Greek mythology, Midas was a wealthy king of Phrygia who believed that more gold would bring him more happiness.

When Midas kindly looked after Silenus, the old teacher of the wine god Dionysus, the grateful god offered him any reward he desired. Without hesitating, Midas asked that everything he touched would turn to gold.

At first the gift seemed wonderful. Twigs, stones and apples glittered in his hands. But when he sat down to dinner, his bread hardened into metal and his wine became liquid gold. The richest man in the world was starving.
Desperate, Midas begged Dionysus to undo the wish. The god told him to wash in the River Pactolus, and according to the myth, that is why the river's sand sparkled with gold ever after.
In a famous later retelling by the American writer Nathaniel Hawthorne, Midas even turns his beloved daughter into a golden statue — a detail that makes the warning hit harder.
Today, the phrase 'the Midas touch' describes someone whose projects always make money, though the original story is really a warning about greed.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Hawthorne wrote the first story about Midas.
The River Pactolus is full of gold today.
Midas's golden wish showed that greed can destroy what truly matters.
Dionysus was the god of gold.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：貪婪的願望毀掉真正重要的東西。

q.q: Why did Dionysus offer Midas a reward?
opts: Midas gave him gold
Midas won a race
Midas was his son
Midas looked after Silenus, his old teacher
q.why: 第二段：Midas kindly looked after Silenus。

He washed in the River Pactolus
He broke his statue
He stopped eating

Because losing someone he loved shows the true cost of greed

c.title: The Poverty of Gold
text: Few myths compress a moral so neatly as that of King Midas. Granted a wish by Dionysus in gratitude for sheltering the god's elderly companion Silenus, the Phrygian king asks that whatever he touches be turned to gold, and discovers at dinner that he has made himself unable to eat.

The story's force lies in its precise inversion. Gold is valuable precisely because it can be exchanged for other things; Midas, by converting everything into gold, abolishes the very things gold was meant to buy. His wealth becomes a form of poverty.

Ancient versions, preserved most famously by the Roman poet Ovid, end with Midas washing away his curse in the River Pactolus, an aetiological flourish explaining the gold-bearing sands of a real river.
Later tellers sharpened the tale. Nathaniel Hawthorne's nineteenth-century version adds a daughter who turns to metal at her father's embrace, shifting the moral from hunger to love.

Curiously, modern English has reversed the myth's meaning. To have 'the Midas touch' is now a compliment for commercial success, as though the cautionary half of the story had been quietly edited out — perhaps the most telling evidence of how persuasive the dream of endless wealth remains.

opts: Midas was a successful businessman.

q.why: 主旨：財富變貧窮的寓言，現代英文卻把警告變成讚美。

q.why: 第二段：把一切變成黃金，反而消滅了黃金能買的東西。

q.q: How does the writer view the modern phrase 'the Midas touch'?
opts: As a correct summary of the myth
As an ironic reversal that reveals how attractive wealth still is
As an insult
As a phrase from Ovid
q.why: 最後一段：反轉神話原意——顯示無盡財富的夢多麼誘人。

q.q: What is the role of paragraph 4 (Hawthorne's version)?
opts: To prove Ovid was wrong
To explain the River Pactolus

To end the essay
q.why: 第四段：shifting the moral from hunger to love。

q.q: An app promises: “Turn all your free time into money!” Based on the essay, what would be the strongest criticism?

topic: World Children's Day: Rights for Every Child
zh: 世界兒童日：每個孩子的權利

a.title: Every Child Has Rights
text: November 20 is World Children's Day. On this day in 1989, the United Nations agreed on a special promise for children.
It is called the Convention on the Rights of the Child. A right is something every person should have.
Children have the right to go to school, to be safe, to see a doctor, and to play.
Children also have the right to give their opinions. Adults should listen when decisions are about them.
Almost every country in the world has signed this promise. Taiwan also made it part of its own laws in 2014.
But many children still cannot go to school or are not safe. World Children's Day reminds us to keep this promise.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How children should play games
World Children's Day and the rights every child should have
Why Taiwan made new laws in 2014

b.title: A Promise to the World's Children
text: On November 20, 1989, the United Nations adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child, and the date is now celebrated as World Children's Day.

The convention sets out the rights that every person under 18 should enjoy, wherever they live. They include the right to education, to health care, to protection from violence and exploitation, and, in a famous article, the right to rest and play.

One of its most important ideas is that children are not just people to be protected. They have the right to express their views on matters that affect them, and adults must take those views seriously.

It has become the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history: every UN member state except the United States has ratified it. Taiwan, which is not a UN member, passed a law in 2014 to make the convention part of its own legal system.
Yet the gap between promise and reality remains wide. Millions of children are still out of school, working in dangerous jobs, or living through war.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: The United States has not ratified the convention.
The 1989 convention promises rights to every child, including a voice, but many children still do not enjoy them.

Only students

c.title: Rights Before Adulthood
text: For most of history, children were regarded less as people than as possessions, or as adults in waiting. The Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted by the UN General Assembly on November 20, 1989, marked a decisive break with that view.

Its premise is that childhood carries rights of its own. Alongside protection from violence, exploitation and neglect, the convention guarantees education, health care and even rest and play, acknowledging that a good childhood is not merely survival.

Its most radical provision concerns participation: children have the right to express their views on matters affecting them, with due weight given according to their age and maturity. This reframes children from passive recipients of care into people whose opinions count.

The treaty has been ratified by every UN member except the United States, making it the most widely accepted human rights agreement ever. Taiwan, excluded from the UN, incorporated it into domestic law in 2014, an example of how norms can spread beyond formal membership.
Ratification, however, is not realisation. Child labour, conflict and unequal schooling persist, a reminder that rights written on paper become real only when adults choose to honour them.

opts: Children are adults in waiting.
The United States wrote the convention.

The convention treats children as rights-holders with a voice, but its promises only become real when adults act on them.
q.why: 主旨：公約視兒童為權利主體並有發聲權，但承諾要靠行動實現。

That a norm can spread even without formal UN membership

That the US followed Taiwan
q.why: 第四段：norms can spread beyond formal membership。
